newsitem.title: USA: Retail sales seen meeting plans, not robust.
newsitem.headline: Retail sales seen meeting plans, not robust.

text.p: Retailers are meeting their sales expectations this holiday season without the sharp markdowns of last year, but sales are not exceptionally strong, retailers and analysts said Monday.
"I'm getting a sense that things are not particularly robust," said William Armstrong, a retailing analyst at Fahnestock & Co. "Last year was terrible and things will be better than they were."
Snowstorms in New England this weekend kept shoppers at home in that region but could spur sales of winter apparel and sporting goods before Christmas, Armstrong said.

Jay Fitzsimmons, senior vice president of finance at Wal-Mart Stores Inc., and other retail executives said this was a difficult period to determine sales trends for the season because the holiday season is shorter this year and customers are doing their gift shopping closer to the holidays.
"We're not sure what to make of numbers we're getting," Fitzsimmons said.

The number of shoppers was close to what Wal-Mart expected, but the average sales receopt showed that shoppers were not buying gifts yet, Fitzsimmons said. He noted that seasonal items, such as Christmas tree decorations, sold well.
"It appears that people are getting ready for Christmas, but they aren't buying gifts yet," Fitzsimmons said.
"We expect to see sales accelerate relative to last year's numbers," Fitzsimmons said.
Laurie Bauer, a spokeswoman at Best Buy Co., said sales for consumer electronics were soft across the industry, but it was too early to tell what the holiday season will hold.

"Thanksgiving weekend was brisk and in line with expectations," Bauer said. Best Buy, Circuit City Stores Inc. and Tandy Corp. each reported weaker November same-store sales, or sales from stores open at least a year.

At Wal-Mart, the nation's largest retailer, Fitzsimmons said, "Our expectation going into the holiday season is comparable-store sales in the 4 to 5 percent range and that is still where we see they are going to be."

A J.C. Penney Co. spokesman said sales were "in line with expectations for the past weekend." The company was expecting total sales growth at its department stores in the mid-single digits for the holiday season, but declined to comment on same-store sales, the company said.
Robert Burton, Kmart Corp. director of investor relations, said sales were "pretty much on plan." The company has spoken about an increase in same-store sales in the 3 percent range, Burton said.
"Our results were very good over Thanksgiving and slightly less strong over the weekend," Burton said, noting that poor weather in the Northeast may have been a factor this weekend.
Kmart reported a November same-store sales increase of 4.1 percent, which excluded the Thanksgiving weekend.
Kmart has not had to resort to sharp markdowns to clear inventory at lower profit margins during the holiday season like they and other retailers did last year, Burton said.

Armstrong said some retailers will use the shorter holiday shopping season as an excuse for poor results. The shopping season between Thanksgiving and Christmas this year is 26 days, five fewer days than last year.
The shorter season should make malls more crowded, but it will decrease impulse purchases, Armstrong said.
"I don't see how that could turn a good season into a bad season," he said.
